clinical: In muscular dystrophies, repeated cycles of fibre damage and repair leave scar-like collagen behind. The perimysium and endomysium thicken with fibrous tissue (fibrosis), so the muscle becomes stiffer and weaker.

The knee-jerk (patellar tendon) reflex depends on Ia sensory endings in muscle spindles. A lost reflex points to a break in the reflex arc, such as a peripheral nerve or nerve-root lesion, while an exaggerated reflex points to an upper motor neuron lesion.

Nerves & vessels.description: Several capillaries surround every muscle fibre, while arterioles and venules run between the fascicles to feed and drain the muscle. Motor nerve branches carry the signal to the fibres and meet each fibre at its motor end plate, the neuromuscular junction.
clinical: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies attack acetylcholine receptors at the motor end plate, so signals cross the neuromuscular junction poorly. This causes weakness that gets worse with repeated use.
If a motor nerve is cut or crushed, the fibres it supplied lose their stimulus and waste away (denervation atrophy), so the muscle weakens.
Nuclei lying in the middle of a fibre, rather than at its edge, are a sign that the fibre was damaged and has regenerated. They are typical of many myopathies.
Rhabdomyolysis is the breakdown of skeletal muscle fibres, releasing myoglobin and creatine kinase into the blood. Myoglobin can cause kidney injury.

Sarcomere.description: A sarcomere is the repeating contractile unit of a myofibril, running from one Z disc to the next. Its thick and thin filaments slide past each other to shorten it, while T tubules carry the electrical signal deep into the fibre and the sarcoplasmic reticulum stores and releases the calcium that triggers contraction.
clinical: Mutations in the RYR1 gene, which encodes the ryanodine receptor on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, can cause malignant hyperthermia. Volatile anaesthetic gases and succinylcholine can trigger uncontrolled calcium release, causing sustained contraction, very high temperature and metabolic crisis.

parts.description: The epimysium is the dense irregular connective-tissue coat of the whole muscle, made mainly of type I collagen. It is continuous inwards with the perimysium and outwards with the tendon and deep fascia, so the pull of every fibre is summed onto the tendon. In a section it is the thick, dense pink outer layer, far coarser than the thin perimysial septa beneath it.

Epimysial collagen bundles are the thick, wavy bundles of type I collagen (the strong collagen of tendon and skin) that make up the epimysium, the outer sheath around a whole muscle. The bundles run in many directions, so the sheath is tough and resists over-stretching, yet it lets the muscle belly widen and shorten as it contracts. In haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections they appear as coarse, dense pink bundles, far thicker than the delicate fibres of the endomysium.

Skeletal muscle fibres are the long, multinucleated cells that make up the muscle belly; each forms by fusion of myoblasts and is about 10–100 µm across. Packed with myofibrils, whose aligned sarcomeres produce the cross-striations, a fibre can run the full length of a muscle, many centimetres in the longest muscles. In transverse section the fibres look polygonal, with nuclei pressed to the edge, and slow oxidative (type I) and fast glycolytic (type II) fibres form an intermixed checkerboard. Grouping of one fibre type suggests denervation followed by reinnervation.

Satellite cells are muscle stem cells, marked by the transcription factor Pax7, lying between the sarcolemma and the basal lamina of a muscle fibre. After injury or intense training they divide, and their progeny fuse into the fibre to repair and enlarge it. In routine sections they are hard to tell from myonuclei, appearing as flattened nuclei pressed against the fibre surface. Their gradual exhaustion is thought to contribute to the progression of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Cardiac muscle has no satellite cells and very little capacity to regenerate.

Endomysial capillaries are the thinnest blood vessels, whose wall is a single layer of endothelial cells, and they run through the endomysium to supply each muscle fibre with oxygen and nutrients. They lie mostly alongside the fibres, joined by cross-links and loops, so every fibre is bathed by several of them. Slow oxidative (type I) fibres have the densest capillary supply, and endurance training increases capillary density. In a longitudinal section they look like fine tubes, often containing single red blood cells, running beside the striated fibres.

Perimysial venules are the small, thin-walled veins of the perimysium, the connective tissue that separates the fascicles, and they collect blood from the capillary beds within each fascicle. Their walls are thinner and less muscular than those of the neighbouring arterioles, so in a section they appear as wide, thin-walled channels, often containing red blood cells, lying beside the arterioles. Their blood drains into larger intramuscular veins, and the squeezing of contracting muscle, working with the valves in those veins, pushes it back towards the heart as the muscle pump.

Myofibrils are the rod-like contractile bundles, about 1–2 µm in diameter, that fill most of the sarcoplasm (cytoplasm) of a muscle fibre. Each myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres joined end to end, and neighbouring myofibrils keep their bands in register, which is why the whole fibre looks cross-striated. Their thick myosin and thin actin filaments slide past one another, so each myofibril shortens and the fibre contracts. In transverse section they appear as many small, closely packed profiles inside the fibre.

The H zone is the paler central part of each A band, where the thick myosin filaments are not overlapped by thin actin filaments, so it looks lighter under the microscope. The M line runs through its centre, and the zone narrows as the thin filaments slide inwards during contraction. At full contraction the thin filaments extend across the whole A band and the H zone disappears.

The M line is a thin line at the centre of the H zone, marking the middle of each sarcomere. It is made of cross-linking proteins, mainly myomesin and M-protein, that hold the thick myosin filaments in a precise, parallel array. Creatine kinase is also concentrated here, where it regenerates ATP from phosphocreatine to keep the contraction going.

The muscle spindle capsule is a thin, spindle-shaped sheath of connective tissue that encloses the specialised intrafusal fibres of a muscle spindle. It is continuous with the perineurium, the connective-tissue wrapping of nerve bundles, and it encloses a fluid-filled periaxial space around the equator of the spindle. The spindle lies within the perimysium, parallel to the ordinary (extrafusal) fibres, and spindles are most numerous in muscles that need fine control, such as those of the hand, neck and eye.

Nuclear bag and chain nuclei are the nuclei of the intrafusal fibres, and their arrangement gives those fibres their names. In nuclear bag fibres the nuclei are crowded into a swollen central region, the equatorial bag, where the sensory endings coil. In the thinner nuclear chain fibres the nuclei sit in a single row, one behind another, along the same central region.
